summary.text: The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation describes how a vehicle moves when it speeds itself up by throwing part of its own mass out at high velocity.
It ties the change in speed to the exhaust velocity and to the ratio of the rocket's starting mass to its final mass.
The mass needed with propellant grows exponentially with the desired delta-v, so a rocket can only carry so much payload.

facts.label: Earlier outline
facts.value: William Moore outlined it as early as 1810

facts.label: Mass growth
facts.value: Needed wet mass grows exponentially with delta-v

facts.label: Famous consequence
facts.value: Called the tyranny of the rocket equation

items.prompt: A team wants to carry twice the cargo, so they simply load far more propellant. Why does this not solve the problem neatly?

options.label: Propellant cannot be added once a design is fixed
The extra propellant adds weight, which raises fuel use further
More propellant slows the exhaust, wasting the gain
Heavier loads make the engine's thrust fall to nothing

items.explain: Higher amounts of propellant add to the overall weight and so increase fuel consumption, which limits the payload a rocket can carry.

items.prompt: A designer wants to size a craft driven by a light sail using Tsiolkovsky's equation. What is the problem?

options.label: Nothing; it works for any craft moving in space
It works only if the sail is small enough
It counts reflected light as double the exhaust
It does not cover systems that are not rockets

items.explain: The equation does not apply to non-rocket systems such as light sails, space elevators or gun launches.

items.prompt: An engineer uses only the bare equation to size the propellant for launching from a planet with an atmosphere, and the figure does not match what the launch needs. What did she leave out?

options.label: Gravity and air drag, which must be added to the delta-v requirement
The exhaust velocity, which the equation does not use
The final mass, which the equation never includes
Nothing, because the equation already counts air and gravity

items.explain: The equation accounts only for the reaction force from the engine, so aerodynamic and gravitational effects must be included in the delta-v requirement.

items.prompt: Moore, Goddard, Oberth and Tsiolkovsky each reached the same formula on their own. What is Tsiolkovsky honored for?

options.label: Being the very first person to work the formula out, ahead of everyone else
Showing that Moore's earlier version of the formula was mistaken
Being first to apply it to whether rockets could reach space-travel speeds
Building the first working rocket that was designed with the formula

items.explain: Moore had derived it earlier, but Tsiolkovsky is honored as the first to apply it to whether rockets could achieve the speeds needed for space travel.

items.prompt: Mission planners ask for a much bigger change in speed from the same engine. What happens to the starting mass needed, propellant included?

options.label: It grows in step with the speed target
It grows exponentially, far faster than the speed target
It stays put, since only exhaust speed matters
It shrinks, because faster rockets are lighter

items.explain: The necessary wet mass grows exponentially with the desired delta-v.

items.prompt: A rocket fires its engine while fighting gravity and drag. Is its delta-v the same as how much its speed actually changed?

options.label: Not always, since gravity and drag also change its speed
Always, since delta-v literally means change in velocity
Always, since gravity and drag cancel each other out
Never, since delta-v only describes the exhaust

items.explain: Gravity and drag also accelerate the vehicle and can add to or subtract from its velocity change, so delta-v may not be the actual change in speed.
